steps.speaker: Young Boy
steps.content: Luminita!

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: It's been a while, kiddo! Have you been good at home? Getting used to living here yet?

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: Oh, the kid's perfectly fine. We're all just glad you're okay, Lumy. That Bureau didn't give you too much trouble, did they?

steps.speaker: Young Boy
steps.content: I'm sorry... It's all because I wasn't clever enough that Luminita got into trouble...

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Hey, what are you talking about? I'm absolutely fine.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: What about all of you, though? Many people from the old district still haven't found new homes, right? And you just went ahead and signed the demolition contracts... Was it because you were worried about me? Or did someone use those hauntings to pressure you?

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: So young, yet so full of worries. But don't fret—there's a new developer in charge now, and we've had every clause checked. The terms are fair, and the compensation should clear any day.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Still, you shouldn't have rushed to sign. You need to stay cautious—who knows if they'll keep their word?

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: Hahaha! If we stayed cautious forever, we'd never get anything done!
The elderly resident casts a deliberate glance toward the door, and Luminita knows that the person who has specifically arranged for her exit today is waiting for her outside.

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: Before, I didn't want to sign the contract. The compensation was part of it, but... leaving the place I've called home for decades wasn't easy. That house holds so many memories, and I had hoped to pass it down to the next generation.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: My grandma used to say the same thing.

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: Yeah, people my age do cling to such things. But when I really thought about it—stubbornly holding onto it just for sentiment, always looking over my shoulder... that's not what a home should be, is it?

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: A house that doesn't give you peace of mind isn't really a home at all.

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: Now that the contract is signed, I actually feel more at ease. We know you and the Chief must have worked hard behind the scenes. We trust you both, and we want to believe we've made the right choice.
The elderly resident gently ruffles the child's hair, a warm smile spreading across her face. Luminita watches, her thoughts adrift in some long-ago memory, before she finally finds her voice again.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: If you have any trouble finding a new place, you absolutely have to come to me!

steps.speaker: Property Owner
steps.content: Of course! We've all kept your business card. When we need a new place, you'll definitely be our first call.
The sound of the door opening and closing echoes from behind. Luminita stands at the doorway, thoughtfully staring at her toes, seemingly lost in contemplation.
Is something still bothering you?

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Oh... no, they all seem to be doing well. By the way, Chief, there's something I don't think I've ever told you in person.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Thank you.
Huh? About what?
Luminita fidgets with the brim of her hat, her gaze skittering away—a rare crack in her usual composure.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: I heard from people at the Bureau that if you hadn't reported those jerks, and if you hadn't kept pushing for new project management and relocation contract revision, this whole situation wouldn't have been resolved so quickly.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: And the fact that I can still come here without any trouble is all thanks to you keeping those haunting rumors under wraps.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: So... thank you. I was wrong to assume you wouldn't help me. I really was too shortsighted, and I'm sorry about that.
Ensuring government projects run smoothly is just part of my job. As for the hauntings... I still have that huge stack of reflection letters you wrote during your detention sitting on my desk.
Given how thorough that punishment was, I'd say we're square.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: We're square, just like that? Well then, I'm going to start bragging to everyone that I've got the MBCC Chief watching my back!
Your response puts Luminita at ease. Her tone becomes light as she glances out the window, then turns back to you with a smile.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Since we've still got time and you're being so accommodating, Chief, I'm going to push my luck and ask for one more favor!

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Why don't you come over to my place? I don't think I've ever told you where I live, have I?
Birds circle in the clear blue sky as sunlight bathes the green landscape around you. Luminita leads you to a scenic garden in Eastside, strolling aimlessly as if on an ordinary walk.
Suddenly she quickens her pace, gets a few steps ahead of you, then turns around with her arms spread wide.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Here we are! Welcome to my home!
You mean... right here?

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: That's right! Remember what I told you before? When I was a kid, my family barely scraped by. Spent most nights on park benches.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: This exact bench right here! Go ahead, say hello to it... Oh come on, don't look at me like that, I'm just kidding!

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: My home really is here. It used to be here.
Luminita sits down on the bench and swings her legs, patting the empty space beside her. After you sit down, she continues.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: See that rock hill on the left? That was the exercise spot back in the day. Every morning, the old-timers would work the parallel bars like they were in the circus. They'd got some real skills!

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: This used to be just an old neighborhood, nothing as pretty as it is now. My grandmother raised me here; lived in these streets long as I can remember.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Then came the demolition notice. Everyone thought it was a good thing at first. Then it turned out the management played us—sweet-talked people into signing the contracts, then kicked us all out.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: And we lost our homes just like that... Even when my grandmother got sick later on, she still blamed herself for being careless and falling for their lies.

She recounts the story with practiced detachment, but her eyes carry an unmistakable weight as they scan the surroundings, as if looking straight through the meticulously maintained garden plants into a distant past.
You decided to help those residents in the old district because you didn't want them to go through what you experienced, right?

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Hmm... I guess you could say that. I just poked my nose where it didn't belong, that's all.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: After all, being homeless in Eastside is a miserable experience. One day you're getting evicted; the next you're freezing under a bridge, never waking up again. Fewer living that nightmare, the better.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: But they're way luckier than I was! They've got someone like you who can actually step in and do something about it. You've really made a difference for them.
She raises her voice to a higher pitch and tilts her head, playfully winking at you. However, you remain unfazed by her calculated attempts at flattery.
Luminita seems unaware that whenever she tries to hide something, she puts on the same mask-like smile to deflect questions.
Beyond the old district situation, why do you go to such lengths to create "haunted houses" and sell them at practically giveaway prices to people who couldn't otherwise afford homes?

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Haven't you asked me this before? It's just business. The "hauntings" are pure marketing, nothing personal.
I did ask before, but this isn't the same. No interrogation room, no official business—just me wanting to know your real answer.

Faking "haunted houses" to turn a profit or stall demolition isn't your only play, or even your best one. With your skills and resources, you could've easily stirred up property rights disputes that'd give developers just as many headaches.
And yet you still chose the haunting approach. Luminita, I'm curious why you're so particularly attached to the idea of "haunted houses."

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: What would knowing all this mean to you anyway?
From an investigative standpoint, it has no particular importance.
But personally speaking... maybe I'm pushing my luck? After all, you did invite me to your "home." That probably means you trust me—at least a little more than before.

Birds still circle overhead in the canopy of sky. After a brief silence, she lets out a sigh—long and slow, part surrender, part relief—like she's finally carved out a small hollow in her burdened heart.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Actually, I've never really thought about why. I've just... kept doing it.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: But if I have to come up with an answer... it's probably just selfishness on my part.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: I want to put my grandmother's soul at ease, and prove to my past self that I can protect my own "home" now, while helping everyone else have a "home" to return to.

steps.speaker: Newscast
steps.content: ...The demolition project has officially launched, with all local residents evacuated and properly resettled. According to municipal planning, to increase urban greenery, this area will soon become the Eastside Scenic Garden, expected to be another landmark attraction for DisCity...
Ding-dong. Ding-dong.
In the early morning, she clutched the old woman's already cold hand. The harsh doorbell of the rental apartment shrieked, but to her, it was muffled, worlds away.
The elderly woman lay still in bed, her coughing silenced, her whispered worries about home and granddaughter finally quieted—as though she had slipped into a dream too deep to break.

steps.speaker: Landlord B
steps.content: Are you deaf? Can't you hear the doorbell? I let it slide last time, but this time you're moving out, whether you like it or—

steps.speaker: Landlord B
steps.content: ...Talk about bad timing. Couldn't she have croaked somewhere else?

A shrill ringing drowned out the landlord's curses, filling her skull like static. Still just a child, she was shoved aside as strangers filed in and out of the room, bombarding her with questions about her personal information.
She had no idea how to respond, frozen in place as she endured the stares—some filled with pity, others hollow with complete indifference.

By the time she came to her senses, officials had already taken her grandmother's body away. The landlord had thrown her out, along with everything the two of them had ever owned, dumping it all outside the door.

steps.speaker: Landlord B
steps.content: If I'd never rented to you lot, I wouldn't be drowning in this cursed bad luck!

steps.speaker: Landlord B
steps.content: Listen up, you little brat. Keep your mouth shut about the death here. If this place gets a "haunted" reputation and I can't rent it out, I swear I'll make you pay for it.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: So I wandered for what felt like ages, dragging my luggage with me. The strap marks on my palms took a whole month to fade.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: The strange thing was, the farther I walked, the lighter my bag felt. I thought I was just toughening up—until I finally found a place to sleep on the street and saw the hole in the bag...
She tries to lighten the mood with a forced smile several times, but each attempt falls flat. Eventually, her gaze drops to her palms, to the long-vanished marks only she remembers.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: As a kid, I was never scared, no matter how late I stayed out playing. Even if I missed the last bus and had to walk those dark, broken-light streets—because I knew Grandma would be waiting, with a light always left on.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: But then, there was nothing left behind me. Just as Grandma had feared—the house was gone, my home was gone, the light went out, and even Grandma was gone. I was left all alone.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: When Grandma's illness got really bad, we couldn't even scrape together money for medicine. She was in so much pain she could barely speak, but all she worried about was still what would happen to me without a home after she was gone.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: So I made up my mind that I'd get my own house someday, even if only to let Grandma rest in peace. I lied about my age to get work, saved every penny I could, and met plenty of others like me along the way.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: But the housing prices in Eastside are impossibly high.
She unconsciously furrows her brow, her hands tightening into fists on her knees.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Most of those places aren't worth half the asking price! Faulty fire alarms and bad drainage are just the start. The worst ones even have crumbling foundations and cracked walls.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: And despite all that, they can still jack up prices and rents to unreasonable levels—enough to scare off anyone who even looks at the listings.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Only those so-called "haunted houses" are different.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: The funny thing? You don't even need a real tragedy. Just a little creative storytelling, some strategic hype, and suddenly those baseless rumors send prices into a nosedive.
Luminita leans forward, her eyes widening as she looks at you, seemingly seeking your validation.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: People break their backs their whole lives, pour every penny into honest work, and still can't afford a home or dig out of mortgage hell. And for what? Places that aren't even half as good as the price tag claims.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: So if a few tricks and some fabricated hauntings can knock prices down and give everyone a place to call home, why wouldn't I play that game?
But these haunted houses you create are ultimately built on lies. And with lies, there's always the risk of being exposed.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: That's just theory. And honestly? Still beats watching people rot on the streets and drift through life.
For every person who can accept that risk, there's someone else who'd lose sleep over it. Besides, not everyone equates a physical property with a "home."
Luminita, you're actually the same way, aren't you?
You keep saying that only a house makes a home, but after you invited me to your "home," you brought me here, to this garden.
The house where you once lived with your grandmother is no longer here, but something else remains that you still consider "home"—something that belongs to you.
She lowers her gaze, her upturned coat collar concealing her expression. Only after a moment do you hear her speak, her words measured and slow.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Earlier, the property owner from the old district said something similar to me.
What?

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: She told me that a house that doesn't give you peace of mind isn't really a home at all. And back at the Bureau, some Sinners turned me down when I tried to sell them houses, saying that they were fine just having the Bureau.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: To be honest, I can't quite wrap my head around it. To me, only a house that's yours carries enough weight to be called a home—walls you own, a key you hold. If you can't trust that, what else in the world can you rely on?

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: But like you said, I've handled so many properties over the years, so why do I end up coming back here?
A gentle breeze blows from behind, slipping through the space between you two on the bench, the whisper of wind nearly drowning out her soft murmuring.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: I've been shoving houses at people, acting like my idea of "home" is universal. Now I wonder... am I really any better than those who inflate property values while pressuring others into homeownership?

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Chief, tell me... have I been wrong about this all along?
This is the closest you've ever come to Luminita's raw heart since you first met her.

Her past experience with forced eviction and the death of a loved one has created an obsession with home ownership that far exceeds normal concerns. Yet this fixation seems to have never filled the hollow place in her heart.

Or maybe that hole isn't empty at all, but rather filled with too many painful memories. And whenever she touches it, she has no defenses left but the raw, child-shaped wound of losing her grandmother—leaving her with no choice but to cling to her obsession.
You can feel Luminita's confusion and uncertainty. For years, she's clung to her grandmother's last words—only a house makes a home—but she's now looking to you for a new truth to follow.
And all you can offer in response is...
I don't know the answer either.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: What do you mean?
Whether you see a house as a home or not, either way is perfectly valid. It's simply a personal choice—what matters is that your choice brings you peace of mind.

Objectively speaking, nothing in this world is truly permanent. You could put down a deposit, only for construction to be abandoned. You could hold the deed and still lose the house to disaster or an accident the very next day.
Nothing material is ever certain. Maybe the true peace of mind only comes from trusting in your own choices.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Sounds like you're just trying to make yourself feel better.
But if it works, why not?

Perhaps someday, you'll return to a place you once stayed, only to find everything you remember is all gone. But the fact that this place was once "home"... it stays with you—in memories, in your bones.
If you choose to believe in those memories, they may become a sanctuary you can return to anytime—something far more lasting than property deeds, only growing more precious with time.
More than whether you owned a house or not, I believe what your grandmother truly cared about was whether you could live in peace.
Then again, that's just how I see it. No need to take it as gospel.
Having said that, you stand up and dust off your clothes, smiling down at Luminita who remains on the bench, looking somewhat dazed.

You're free to believe what you want, and I won't deny Eastside's real estate has many serious problems that need addressing. However, that doesn't mean I can justify your methods of fabricating hauntings.
Still, I look forward to the day when the Bureau becomes a place where you can say "I'm home" when you walk through the door.
That would make me very happy.
Your revealing statement makes Luminita narrow her eyes instinctively. She stands up and moves closer, her face now inches from yours.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: So... can I still come back even after doing something bad? Would you still take me in if I walked up and said, "Hey Chief, I just tied up three Corruptors today to haunt a house"?
...Then it won't be as simple as just confinement and written reflection.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: That whole speech you just gave me is part of your plan to stop me from pestering you about buying a house, isn't it?
I didn't realize there was that interpretation. Can't believe you saw right through me.
The girl can no longer contain herself and bursts into hearty laughter.

After her laughter subsides, she looks at you with newfound ease, like a river freed at last from the final obstruction after years of blockage. The current still stutters, but the truth is undeniable: given time, it will run smooth and clear.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Thank you. Changing my ways won't happen overnight, but I'll try.

steps.speaker: Luminita
steps.content: Well, then I'll also look forward to the day you greet me with "Welcome back" at the Bureau.
The soaring bird finally folds its wings and perches on the evergreen tree beside the bench.

Soon after, the personal investigation into Luminita concludes, confirming that her harboring of Corruptors was solely to create paranormal phenomena in "haunted houses" with no intent to harm people. The Bureau consequently reassesses her threat level.
Considering the nature of Luminita's work and her personal wishes, you apply for her bail.
The day her bail processes, you arrive at the detention area only to find her gone. But the room isn't empty—belongings she deliberately chose not to take are still scattered throughout.
On the desk, pinned beneath a book, rests a scrap of paper torn to business-card size. A single line of text stares up, followed by a phone number, all in wildly scrawled handwriting.
"Personal business card with my private contact info."
"I'll be back to stay for a few days once I wrap up this job. Don't throw my stuff away!"
